Comments for authors:
This paper fits models to spike trains of retinal ganglion cells that are driven by natural images. I think the title should thus include the word “activity” at the end for otherwise it is actually formally incorrect.

Anyhow, this paper proposes more specifically a recurrent network for this time series prediction and compares it to what seems to be the previous approach of a generalized linear model. Overall the stated paradigm is that when one can predict the spikes well then one can look into the model and learn how nature does it. 

In general the paper sounds plausible, though I am not convinced that I learned a lot. The results in figure 2 show that the RNN model can predict the spikes a bit better. So this is nice. But now what? You have shown that a more complicated model can produce better fits to the data, though there are of course still some variations to the real data. Your initial outline was that a better predictive model helps you to better understand the neural processing in the retina. So tell us what you learned. I am not a specialist of the retina, but I know that there are several layers and recurrencies in the retina, so I am not so surprised that the new model is better than the GLM. 

It seems that more complicated recurrent models such as LSTM do not improve the performance according to a statement in the paper. However, comparisons on this level are also difficult as a more complex models needs more data. Hence, I would actually expect that more layers and even a more detailed model of the retina could eventually improve the prediction even further. 
I was also a bit puzzled that all the neurons in the network share all the same parameters (weights). While the results show that these simplified models can capture a lot of the spike train characteristics, couldn’t a model with free parameters eventually outperform this one (with correspondingly more training data)?

Summary: This paper applies multitask recurrent neural networks to the problem of predicting spiking responses of primate retinal ganglion cells to natural image stimuli. The authors fit two-layer RNNs with parameters shared across neurons and compare them against standard linear-nonlinear (LN) and generalized linear models (GLMs). They find that the RNNs consistently capture a larger fraction of explainable variance across both ON and OFF parasol cells in two separate experimental preparations. To understand the source of this improvement, the authors introduce a GLM-RNN hybrid model in which a linear spatial filter precedes recurrent temporal processing. This hybrid recovers a substantial portion of the performance gap, suggesting that richer temporal nonlinearities account for much of the RNN advantage, though spatial nonlinearities also contribute. The paper further demonstrates that the multitask framework yields more accurate and stable predictions than individually trained RNNs, and that good predictive performance can be achieved with surprisingly small amounts of training data.

Strengths: The paper tackles a timely and important problem at the interface of machine learning and computational neuroscience. The experimental analysis is rigorous and includes several well-designed controls, such as ablating receptive field patch size, comparing shared versus individual model training, and constructing the hybrid architecture to disentangle spatial and temporal contributions. The finding that multitask parameter sharing improves generalization in a data-limited neurophysiology setting is practically significant and well-supported by the results. The manuscript is clearly written, the methods are described in sufficient detail to permit reproduction, and the analysis of training data requirements addresses a key practical concern for applying deep learning to neural data. Overall, the study provides a convincing demonstration that flexible recurrent architectures can outperform classical models in sensory neuroscience.

Weaknesses: The network architectures explored are relatively standard, and the methodological novelty is limited primarily to the application domain rather than to learning algorithms or architectures. Despite the hybrid model, the internal computations of the full RNN remain largely uninterpreted, and the paper does not provide a detailed analysis of the specific temporal features or dynamics that the recurrent layers capture. The study is restricted to parasol ganglion cells from only two retinal preparations, which raises questions about how well the conclusions generalize to other retinal cell types, other species, or cortical circuits. The use of mean squared error on smoothed firing rates, rather than a point-process likelihood, is a questionable choice for modeling discrete spike trains, even though the authors note that Poisson likelihood optimization gave qualitatively similar results. Finally, the paper explicitly ignores correlations between neurons, which are known to carry substantial information in the retina; incorporating at least simple coupling terms could have strengthened the modeling framework.

Questions for the authors: How sensitive are the main conclusions to the choice of loss function, and would optimizing a Poisson or other point-process likelihood alter the relative ranking of the models or the interpretation of the hybrid results? Could you provide more concrete visualizations or examples of the temporal nonlinearities captured by the hybrid model that are absent in the GLM? Have you considered whether more biologically plausible constraints, such as localized connectivity or divisive normalization in the recurrent layers, would preserve performance while improving interpretability? How does model performance compare when trained on white noise versus natural scene stimuli, and does the RNN advantage persist across stimulus classes? Finally, what do you see as the main obstacle to extending this multitask RNN approach to larger, more heterogeneous neural populations or to cortical areas?

Recommendation: I recommend this paper for acceptance. While the architectures themselves are not novel, the work makes a solid empirical contribution by showing that multilayer recurrent networks and multitask learning can substantially improve predictive models of neural spiking responses. The careful experimental design, the practical insights for neuroscience, and the clear presentation make this a valuable paper for the ICLR audience. I would assign an overall score of 6, indicating a good paper that should be accepted, though not without the minor limitations noted above.

This paper explores whether nonlinear recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can account for neural response properties that have eluded other models. A multilayer RNN is trained to mimic the stimulus-response mapping observed in actual retinal ganglion cells responding to a sequence of natural images. The RNN performs significantly better than conventional LN/GLM models, particularly in capturing transient responses.

This work represents an important step toward understanding the nonlinear response properties of visual neurons. Recent results have shown that even the responses of retinal ganglion cells to natural movies are difficult to explain using standard receptive field models, presenting a significant challenge to the field. Even having *a* model that works would be a starting point, so this work should be viewed in that light. The challenge now, of course, is to determine what the RNN is actually doing. Perhaps it could be pruned and simplified to identify which components are critical to its performance; it would have been nice to see such an analysis. Nevertheless, this result is a promising first step and, in my view, important for the community to know about.

Review for ICLR 2017

Summary:
The paper proposes a method for neural network compression based on "soft weight-sharing," a technique originally introduced by Nowlan and Hinton in 1992. The authors frame the problem through the lens of the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle, treating compression as a variational inference problem. Specifically, they model the weight prior as a mixture of Gaussians (GMM) and learn the mixture parameters (means, variances, and mixing proportions) simultaneously with the network weights using gradient descent. This approach allows the network to automatically determine the optimal number of clusters and the pruning rate (by fixing one component at zero). The final compression is achieved by quantizing weights to the nearest cluster mean and utilizing storage formats similar to those used by Han et al. (2015).

Strengths:
1. Theoretical Grounding: The paper provides a clear and principled connection between variational learning, the MDL principle, and model compression.
2. Unified Approach: The method integrates pruning and quantization into a single training procedure, rather than relying on the multi-step pipeline (pruning then quantizing) common in other state-of-the-art methods.
3. Flexibility: By learning the prior, the model can adaptively determine the necessary quantization intervals and the amount of pruning required per layer.
4. Strong Results on Small Models: The authors achieve state-of-the-art compression rates on MNIST-based models (LeNet) with negligible loss in accuracy.

Weaknesses:
1. Limited Scalability: The experimental results are primarily focused on small models. While a ResNet is mentioned, the authors admit that the algorithm is too slow for larger architectures like VGG. The proposed solution for scalability (sampling weights for the prior gradient) is discussed in the appendix but not experimentally validated.
2. Hyper-parameter Sensitivity: The authors note that the learning rates for the mixture components are "very sensitive" and that the mixture can collapse too quickly. The reliance on Bayesian optimization (Spearmint) to tune 13 different hyperparameters suggests that the method may be difficult to apply to new architectures without significant tuning effort.
3. Baseline Comparisons: While the results on LeNet are strong, the lack of comprehensive results on larger, modern datasets (like ImageNet) makes it difficult to assess if the method remains competitive against the highly optimized pipelines of Han et al. on complex tasks.
4. Implementation Complexity: The retraining process requires managing separate learning rates and potential hyper-priors (Inverse-Gamma, Beta) to prevent component collapse, which increases implementation complexity compared to simple post-training quantization.

Questions for the authors:
1. Regarding the scalability issue: You propose sampling K weights to approximate the prior gradient in Appendix C. Have you performed any preliminary tests to see if this maintains the same compression quality as the full gradient?
2. How does the total training time (including the Bayesian optimization phase) compare to the pipeline proposed by Han et al.?
3. You mentioned that the amount of pruning depends on the number of parameters in the layer. Do you have a theoretical explanation for why larger layers are more amenable to pruning in this framework?
4. Could you clarify the impact of the choice of the initial number of components (e.g., 17 for LeNet vs 64 for ResNet)? Is there a heuristic for choosing this number for an unknown architecture?

Recommendation:
Accept (Poster). The paper presents a mathematically sound and elegant way to unify pruning and quantization through the MDL principle. Although the experimental section is dominated by smaller models and the scalability to very large networks is not yet proven, the conceptual contribution is significant and provides a principled alternative to heuristic-based compression pipelines.

This paper proposes an empirical Bayesian approach to learn the parameters of a neural network and their corresponding priors. A mixture model prior over the weights leads to a clustering effect in the weight posterior distributions (which are approximated with delta peaks). This clustering effect can be exploited for the quantization and compression of network parameters. The authors demonstrate that this method achieves compression rates and predictive accuracies comparable to related approaches.

Earlier work [Han et al. 2015] is based on a three-stage process: pruning small-magnitude weights, clustering the remaining ones, and updating the cluster centers to optimize performance. The current work provides a more principled approach that avoids this ad-hoc multi-stage structure in favor of a single iterative optimization process.

The first experiment, described in Section 6.1, shows that an empirical Bayes approach—even without hyper-priors—already leads to a pronounced clustering effect and sets many weights to zero. In particular, a compression rate of 64.2 is obtained on the LeNet300-100 model. Note that in Section 6.1, the text refers to "Figure C," which I assume should be "Figure 1."

Section 6.2 describes an experiment where hyper-priors are used, and the parameters of these distributions, as well as other hyper-parameters like learning rates, are optimized using Spearmint (Snoek et al., 2012). Figure 2 shows the performance of different points evaluated in the hyper-parameter space (each trained network represents an accuracy-compression rate point on the graph). The text claims that the best results lie on a line; this seems a somewhat interpretation given the limited data. Moreover, it would be useful to add a brief discussion on whether such a linear relationship would be expected. Currently, the results of this experiment lack sufficient interpretation.

Section 6.3 presents results for CNN models and compares them to recent findings by Han et al. (2015) and Guo et al. (2016). Comparable results are obtained in terms of compression rate and accuracy. The authors state that their current algorithm is too slow to be useful for larger models such as VGG-19, though they briefly report some results for this model (without comparing them to related work). It would be helpful to explain what slows down the training compared to standard training without weight clustering, and how the proposed algorithm scales with respect to data volume and model size.

The contribution of this paper is largely experimental, leveraging standard ideas from empirical Bayesian learning to introduce weight clustering effects into CNN training. That said, it is an interesting result that such a relatively straightforward approach leads to results on par with state-of-the-art, yet more ad-hoc, network compression techniques. The paper could be improved by clearly describing the training algorithm and how it scales to large networks and datasets. Another point deserving further discussion is how the hyper-parameter search is performed (I assume test data is not used) and how the compared methods handled the search over hyper-parameters to determine the accuracy-compression tradeoff. Ideally, methods should be evaluated across multiple points on this trade-off curve.
